summary: The most massive single-stem tree on Earth. General Sherman, in Sequoia National Park, holds roughly 1,487 cubic metres of wood, and the oldest sequoias counted by rings passed 3,000 years. Its bark, up to about 90 cm thick at the base and nearly resin-free, lets it shrug off the low fires its cones depend on.
nativeRange: About 70 scattered groves on the western slope of the Sierra Nevada, California, at 1,400–2,000 m
abilities: Grows fibrous, tannin-rich bark up to about 90 cm thick that insulates the cambium from surface fires
Keeps cones closed and green on the tree for up to 20 years; heat from fire, Douglas squirrels and a cone-boring beetle release the seeds
Seedlings need bare mineral soil and open sky, conditions that low-intensity fire creates
Reaches the largest trunk volume of any tree: General Sherman is about 83.8 m tall and 11 m across at the base
edibilityNote: No part is eaten. Not known to be significantly toxic.

fruit.season: Matures over two seasons; may persist green for many years
fruit.description: Egg-sized cones 4–7 cm long, holding about 200 seeds each.

seed.dispersal: Wind, after cones are dried by fire or chewed open by squirrels and beetles
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 4–8 weeks; sow on the surface of bare, moist mineral soil

grow.timeToHarvest: Ornamental; cones begin at around 10–20 years
steps: Stratify seed in moist sand in the fridge for 4–8 weeks
Surface-sow in a free-draining mix and keep evenly moist and bright
Pot on yearly and plant out at 1–3 years where it has room to become enormous
Avoid planting near buildings: roots spread widely and the crown becomes massive

lore: Specimens were stripped and shipped east for exhibition in the 1850s, and the outcry over the felled 'Discovery Tree' helped lead Lincoln to sign the 1864 Yosemite Grant, an early act of American wilderness protection. Fires in 2020–2021 killed an estimated 13–19% of all large sequoias.
funFact: Despite its fire-proof reputation, the 2020 Castle Fire alone killed an estimated 7,500–10,600 large sequoias, about a tenth of the world's mature population.

summary: The tallest living thing known. Hyperion, found in Redwood National Park in 2006, measured about 116 m, taller than a 35-storey building. Redwoods drink fog through their leaves, sprout new trunks from burls, and grow whole hanging gardens in their crowns.
nativeRange: A narrow fog belt along the Pacific coast from south-western Oregon to Big Sur, California
abilities: Absorbs fog water directly through its foliage, which matters in rainless California summers
Resprouts from basal burls and root crowns after fire or felling, forming 'fairy rings' of clones
Builds canopy soils that support ferns, huckleberries and even other trees high above the ground
Has a hexaploid genome, with six sets of chromosomes, unusual among conifers
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Not considered significantly toxic.

fruit.description: Olive-sized cones 1.5–3 cm long that release tiny seeds.

seed.description: Tiny two-winged brown seeds, mostly of low viability
seed.dispersal: Wind; most regeneration is clonal sprouting
seed.germination: No pretreatment needed; sow on moist mix, germination often under 10%

grow.timeToHarvest: Ornamental or timber; cones from 5–15 years
steps: Sow fresh seed in spring on moist, sterile mix (expect low germination)
Keep seedlings humid and sheltered from drying wind
Plant out in deep soil and water through dry summers for the first years
Give it space: it can add 1 m or more a year in good conditions

lore: Old-growth logging after the 1849 Gold Rush removed about 95% of the original redwood forest; the Save the Redwoods League, founded in 1918, began buying groves back. The Yurok and Tolowa used fallen redwood for plank houses and dugout canoes.
funFact: Hyperion's exact location is kept quiet, and since 2022 visitors who go off-trail to find it risk a fine of up to $5,000 and up to six months in jail.

summary: Among the oldest individual non-clonal organisms on Earth. The tree called Methuselah, in California's White Mountains, germinated more than 4,800 years ago, before the Great Pyramid was finished. Bristlecones survive by growing incredibly slowly and letting most of their bark die back.
nativeRange: High mountains of eastern California, Nevada and Utah, mostly 2,600–3,500 m
abilities: Lives more than 4,800 years on dry, alkaline dolomite where few competitors grow
Practises 'sectored architecture': when roots die, only the matching strip of bark dies, so the tree survives on a narrow living ribbon
Produces dense, resinous wood that resists rot, insects and fungi, so dead wood can lie on the ground for thousands of years
Keeps needles for up to 40 years or more, saving energy on dry ground
edibilityNote: Pine seeds are small and not a traditional food; not considered toxic.

fruit.description: Dark purple cones 6–10 cm long with a fragile bristle on each scale.

seed.description: Small seeds with a detachable wing
seed.dispersal: Wind, and caching by Clark's nutcrackers
seed.germination: Cold-stratify ~60 days; sow in gritty mineral mix

steps: Cold-stratify seed for about two months
Sow in a gritty, low-nutrient mix
Grow on in full sun with minimal fertilizer
Plant in poor, well-drained ground; rich soil and wet roots kill it

lore: Edmund Schulman's ring-counts in the 1950s revealed the trees' age, and bristlecone chronologies stretching back more than 8,000 years were used to calibrate radiocarbon dating. In 1964 a researcher cut down the tree later named Prometheus, at about 4,900 years old, with Forest Service permission.
funFact: Because bristlecone ring-widths record past climate, the trees helped show that early radiocarbon dates were off by centuries.

summary: A tree that becomes a forest. Banyans drop aerial roots from their branches that thicken into new trunks, so one individual can spread across more than a hectare. India's national tree, it has shaded village councils, markets and teachers for millennia.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent; planted across the tropics
abilities: Turns hanging aerial roots into pillar trunks, letting a single tree expand indefinitely
Often starts life as an epiphyte from a bird-dropped seed, then strangles and replaces its host
Thimmamma Marrimanu in Andhra Pradesh covers about 1.9 hectares from a single tree
Fruits year-round in many places, feeding birds, bats and monkeys when little else is fruiting
Relies on a single fig-wasp species, Eupristina masoni, for pollination
edibilityNote: Ripe figs are edible but bland and often contain fig wasps. The milky latex irritates skin and eyes.

uses.use: Bark and aerial roots (vata) used as astringents for diarrhoea and in preparations for diabetes
Latex applied to cracked heels, sores and toothache

medicinal.cautions: Latex is a skin and eye irritant and can cause allergy in people sensitive to Ficus or latex.

fruit.description: Paired, cherry-sized figs that ripen scarlet, borne in leaf axils.

seed.dispersal: Birds, bats and monkeys; seeds often germinate in tree crowns or walls
seed.germination: Surface-sow on moist mix, warm and bright; 2–4 weeks

steps: Root a semi-ripe cutting or air-layer a branch in warm, humid conditions
Plant far from buildings, drains and walls
Guide young aerial roots into the ground (in pipes of soil if needed) to form pillars
Indoors it can be kept as a pot plant or bonsai

lore: The banyan is the tree of the Hindu fast Vat Purnima, when married women tie threads around it in memory of Savitri, who won back her husband's life from Yama. The English word comes from 'banias', the Hindu merchants Portuguese and English traders saw trading under its shade.
funFact: The Great Banyan in Howrah's botanic garden lost its main trunk to fungal rot in 1925 yet still stands as a ring of more than 3,000 aerial-root trunks.

summary: The tree under which Siddhartha Gautama is said to have attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya. Its heart-shaped leaves end in a long 'drip tip' that sheds rain, and they tremble in the slightest breeze. A cutting planted in Sri Lanka in 288 BCE is still alive.
nativeRange: Indian subcontinent and Indochina; planted at temples across Asia
abilities: Leaves taper into a long drip tip that channels rain off the leaf
Germinates on walls, temples and other trees and pries masonry apart with its roots
Pollinated only by its own fig wasp, Platyscapa quadraticeps
Lives for many centuries; the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi has a documented history of more than 2,300 years
edibleParts: young leaves and shoots (cooked, famine food)
edibilityNote: Small figs are eaten but usually contain fig wasps. The latex is an irritant.

uses.use: Bark decoction for skin problems, wounds and diarrhoea; fruit for asthma
Bark and latex for inflammation and gum problems

medicinal.cautions: Latex can irritate skin and eyes and cause allergy.

fruit.description: Pea-sized paired figs that ripen dark purple.

seed.germination: Surface-sow on moist mix in warmth and light

steps: Root a cutting or air-layer in warm, humid conditions
Pot on in free-draining mix in bright light
Plant away from walls and foundations, which its roots crack
In cool climates grow as a large houseplant or bonsai

lore: Emperor Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta is said to have carried a cutting of the Bodh Gaya tree to Anuradhapura, where King Devanampiya Tissa planted it in 288 BCE; it is often called the oldest human-planted tree with a recorded planting date. Hindus circle the peepal and tie threads around it; it is the ashvattha of the Bhagavad Gita (15.1), the cosmic tree with roots above and branches below.
funFact: The tree at Bodh Gaya today is traditionally said to descend from the one in Sri Lanka, so the Sri Lankan tree is in effect the 'parent' of its own ancestor's replacement.

summary: The last survivor of an order of trees that goes back more than 290 million years, often called a living fossil. Its fan-shaped leaves look much like Jurassic fossils, and several trees near the Hiroshima hypocentre survived the 1945 bombing and still leaf out every spring.
nativeRange: Possibly wild populations in Zhejiang and Guizhou/Chongqing, China; planted worldwide
abilities: Has motile, swimming sperm with thousands of flagella, discovered in 1896 by Sakugoro Hirase
Tolerates air pollution, compacted soil and road salt, making it a favourite street tree
Has very few insect pests or diseases
Lives for well over 1,000 years; some temple trees in China are estimated at 3,000+ years
edibilityNote: Only the cooked kernel is eaten, and only a few at a time. Kernels contain ginkgotoxin (4′-O-methylpyridoxine), which can cause vomiting and seizures, especially in children who eat many; raw kernels are riskier. The smelly fleshy seed coat holds ginkgolic acids that cause poison-ivy-like dermatitis, so wear gloves.

uses.use: Seeds for cough, asthma and urinary frequency
Standardised leaf extract (e.g. EGb 761) studied for dementia, memory and circulation

medicinal.cautions: Leaf extract may raise bleeding risk with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs and before surgery. Seeds can cause poisoning and seizures; the seed coat causes contact dermatitis.

fruit.description: Apricot-like seeds on female trees with a yellow outer coat that smells of rancid butter (butyric acid).

seed.description: Hard, cream-coloured inner shell around a green kernel, inside a fleshy outer coat
seed.dispersal: Falls; probably once carried by animals that are now extinct
seed.germination: Clean the flesh off with gloves, cold-stratify 1–3 months, sow 2–3 cm deep

grow.propagation: Seed, cuttings, grafting (male clones for streets)
grow.timeToHarvest: Female trees bear seed after 20–35 years
steps: Clean the seed with gloves and stratify it in damp sand in the fridge
Sow in deep pots, since it makes a long taproot
Grow in full sun; growth is slow for the first few years
Plant grafted male clones if you don't want the smelly seeds

lore: Monks kept ginkgo alive for centuries in temple gardens in China, Korea and Japan; Engelbert Kaempfer described it for Europe after visiting Japan in the 1690s. Goethe sent a pressed leaf with his 1815 poem 'Ginkgo biloba', using its split leaf as an image of one being that is also two.
funFact: The odd spelling 'Ginkgo' was long blamed on a misprint by Engelbert Kaempfer; later research suggests it reflects how his Nagasaki interpreter pronounced 'ginkyō'.

summary: A plant that grows just two leaves in its whole life, which can be more than a thousand years. The leaves keep growing from the base like conveyor belts while the tips fray in the Namib wind. It is the only species in its family, a gymnosperm lineage that branched off over 100 million years ago.
nativeRange: Namib Desert of western Namibia and south-western Angola
abilities: Grows only two strap-shaped leaves, which lengthen continuously from a basal meristem for its whole life
Large plants are estimated by radiocarbon at 1,000–2,000 years old
Survives where rain may not fall for years, drawing on fog and a deep taproot
Its genome carries signs of an ancient duplication and stress-tolerance adaptations linked to its longevity
edibilityNote: The core was reportedly eaten raw or roasted in hard times by local peoples, but it is protected and should not be harvested.

fruit.type: Cones (male and female on separate plants)
fruit.season: Mostly spring and summer after rare rain
fruit.description: Female plants bear blue-green to salmon cones; male cones are smaller and salmon-coloured.

seed.dispersal: Wind; establishment only after unusual rains
seed.germination: Sow fresh on sandy mix at 25–30 °C; fungal rot is the main killer

grow.water: Low but regular in deep pots
steps: Dust fresh seed with fungicide and sow in a very deep pot of sterile sand
Keep at 25–30 °C and lightly moist until germination (1–3 weeks)
Never transplant: the taproot hates disturbance
Give strong sun and water deeply but infrequently

lore: Austrian botanist Friedrich Welwitsch found it in southern Angola in 1859 and reportedly knelt and stared, afraid it would vanish if he touched it; Joseph Hooker described it in 1863. It appears on Namibia's national coat of arms.
funFact: Each plant has only two true leaves; the many 'leaves' you see are those two, split lengthwise by wind into ribbons.

otherNames: Dam al-akhawayn ('blood of the two brothers', Arabic)
summary: An umbrella-shaped tree found only on the island of Socotra, whose bark bleeds a deep red resin, the 'dragon's blood' traded across the ancient world. Its dense, upturned crown catches mist and shades its own roots in a harsh, dry climate.
nativeRange: Endemic to the Socotra archipelago, Yemen
abilities: Its umbrella crown condenses mist and funnels water down the branches while shading the soil
Exudes a red resin (dragon's blood) when the bark is cut
Survives on fog and monsoon moisture on dry limestone plateaus
Shades seedlings of other species, creating micro-habitats on bare ground
edibilityNote: Not a food; resin is used medicinally and as a dye. Livestock graze seedlings.

uses.use: Resin applied to wounds and burns and taken for diarrhoea and fevers
Resin as an astringent for wounds and eye problems

medicinal.cautions: Commercial 'dragon's blood' often comes from other species (Daemonorops, Croton); identity varies.

fruit.description: Small orange-red berries eaten by birds.

seed.germination: Sow fresh in warm, free-draining mix; germination slow

steps: Sow fresh seed in gritty mix at 25 °C
Grow on in bright light, letting it dry between waterings
Keep frost-free; overwatering causes rot
Be patient: it may take decades to branch

lore: Socotra's resin is thought to be the 'cinnabar' of Pliny and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. A Socotri legend says the trees first grew from the blood of two brothers who fought to the death.
funFact: It branches only when its growing tip stops, usually after flowering, so the forks of its umbrella crown record the tree's flowering history.

summary: One of the largest single flowers on Earth, up to about a metre across and weighing up to roughly 11 kg. Rafflesia has no leaves, stems or roots: it lives as threads inside a jungle vine and appears only when a cabbage-like bud bursts through the bark and opens into a flower that smells of rotting meat.
nativeRange: Rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo
abilities: Is a holoparasite with no leaves, stem, roots or chlorophyll, living as cell strands inside Tetrastigma vines
Produces flowers up to about 1 m across, the largest single flowers known
Mimics a carcass in colour, texture and smell to attract carrion flies as pollinators
Has lost its chloroplast genome, and has taken up many genes from its host by horizontal gene transfer
edibilityNote: Not eaten as food. Buds are harvested in some areas for traditional medicine, which threatens wild populations.

fruit.description: Round, rough fruit with oily pulp and thousands of tiny seeds.

seed.dispersal: Probably small mammals such as tree shrews, and ants
seed.germination: Only on Tetrastigma host vines; how infection happens is poorly understood

lore: A guide working for Joseph Arnold and Stamford Raffles found it in Sumatra in 1818; Arnold died shortly afterward and the plant was named after both men. It is one of Indonesia's three national flowers.
funFact: Each flower lasts only about five to seven days, after a bud that took roughly nine months to a year to develop.

summary: The largest unbranched inflorescence in the plant world, rising up to about 3 m from a corm that can weigh more than 150 kg. When it blooms it heats its central spike and pumps out a stench of rotting flesh to draw carrion beetles and flies through the Sumatran forest.
nativeRange: Equatorial rainforest of western Sumatra, Indonesia
abilities: Heats its spadix (thermogenesis) to near human body temperature, helping the scent spread
Releases sulfur compounds such as dimethyl trisulfide that smell like a carcass
Stores energy in a giant corm; a record corm at Edinburgh weighed 153.9 kg in 2010
Between blooms it grows a single huge leaf that can reach about 6 m, like a small tree
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Like many aroids its tissues contain calcium oxalate crystals, which burn the mouth if eaten raw.

fruit.description: Hundreds of olive-sized berries ripen from yellow to red.

seed.description: One or two seeds per berry
seed.dispersal: Birds such as hornbills eat the berries
seed.germination: Sow fresh (seeds don't store) in warm, humid mix

grow.water: High while in leaf; reduce during dormancy
grow.propagation: Fresh seed, or leaf cuttings in specialist collections
steps: Sow fresh seed immediately in warm, humid conditions
Pot the corm into progressively larger containers as it grows
Keep humid and warm (24–30 °C) year-round
Let the leaf die back naturally and rest the corm before regrowth

lore: Italian botanist Odoardo Beccari sent seeds to Europe after finding it in 1878, and it first bloomed in cultivation at Kew in 1889. David Attenborough coined 'titan arum' for his BBC series The Private Life of Plants, finding the Latin name too rude for television.
funFact: The Latin name means 'giant misshapen phallus'.

summary: A plant that counts. Its hinged leaf-traps snap shut in about a tenth of a second, but only after two touches of the trigger hairs within about 20 seconds, and it starts making digestive enzymes only after more touches. In the wild it grows only in a small area of the Carolinas.
nativeRange: Coastal plain wetlands within roughly 120 km of Wilmington, North and South Carolina
abilities: Snaps its trap in about 100 milliseconds using stored elastic energy that flips the leaf's curvature
Counts trigger-hair touches: two to close, five or so to start full digestion
Sends electrical action potentials through the leaf, much like a nerve
Gets nitrogen and phosphorus from prey, which lets it grow in very poor, boggy soils
Depends on regular fire to keep competing plants from shading it
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Not significantly toxic.

fruit.description: Small capsules on a tall stalk, held well above the traps so pollinators are not caught.

seed.germination: Surface-sow on damp peat-sand; 2–4 weeks in light and warmth

grow.water: Constantly moist with rainwater or distilled water only
grow.soil: Unfertilised sphagnum peat with sand or perlite
steps: Pot in pure peat and perlite (no fertiliser, no potting compost)
Stand the pot in a tray of rainwater in full sun
Never use tap water with dissolved minerals and never fertilise the soil
Give a cool winter dormancy (around 0–10 °C) for 3–4 months

lore: Governor Arthur Dobbs of North Carolina described it in 1759, and Charles Darwin called it 'one of the most wonderful plants in the world' in Insectivorous Plants (1875). Since 2014, poaching wild flytraps in North Carolina has been a felony.
funFact: Small insects that can wriggle out between the 'teeth' are released on purpose; the trap does not seal for prey too small to be worth digesting.

summary: Maker of the largest pitchers of any carnivorous plant, up to about 40 cm tall and holding litres of fluid. It catches insects, but also gets nitrogen from tree shrews that sit on the rim to lick nectar from the lid and leave their droppings in the pitcher.
nativeRange: Endemic to Mount Kinabalu and Mount Tambuyukon, Sabah, Malaysian Borneo, about 1,500–2,650 m
biomes: Montane ultramafic grassland and forest edges
abilities: Forms urn-shaped pitchers big enough to hold several litres of fluid
Feeds mountain tree shrews (Tupaia montana) with lid nectar, and the pitcher fits a tree shrew's body exactly
Its slippery rim (peristome) sends insects into digestive fluid
Grows on serpentine (ultramafic) soils rich in metals and poor in nutrients
Occasionally traps frogs, lizards or rats
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Protected species.

fruit.description: Narrow capsules on a tall raceme, plants are male or female.

seed.germination: Surface-sow fresh on milled sphagnum, high humidity, cool nights

grow.soil: Open mix of sphagnum, bark, perlite and pumice
grow.propagation: Tissue culture or seed (wild collection is illegal)
steps: Buy legal tissue-cultured plants (it is on CITES Appendix I)
Keep days around 20–25 °C and nights about 10–15 °C
Give 70–90% humidity and rainwater only
Don't fertilise the medium; an occasional insect in a pitcher is enough

lore: Hugh Low collected it on Kinabalu in 1858 and Joseph Hooker named it in 1859 for James Brooke, the 'White Rajah' of Sarawak. Victorian nurseries such as Veitch sent collectors to Borneo for these plants.
funFact: The opening of the pitcher matches a tree shrew's body length, so the animal sits where its droppings fall straight into it.

summary: A small bog plant whose leaves are covered in red tentacles, each tipped with a drop of sticky 'dew'. Insects that land get stuck, the tentacles slowly bend over them, and the leaf digests them. Darwin spent years experimenting on it.
nativeRange: Circumboreal: Europe, northern Asia, North America, Greenland
abilities: Its glandular tentacles secrete sticky mucilage that traps insects
Bends tentacles, and sometimes the whole leaf, around struggling prey over minutes to hours
Secretes digestive enzymes and absorbs nitrogen from prey
Survives harsh winters as a tight bud (hibernaculum)
edibilityNote: Not a food. Historically used to flavour liqueur and curdle milk.

uses.use: Herb tea or tincture for dry and spasmodic coughs and whooping cough
Remedy for coughs (homeopathic preparations contain essentially no plant material)

medicinal.cautions: Wild collection is restricted in many countries; most commercial Drosera is other species. Naphthoquinones irritate skin.

fruit.description: Tiny capsules on a slender stalk well above the leaves.

seed.germination: Cold-stratify 4–8 weeks; surface-sow on damp peat in light

steps: Sow stratified seed on damp peat or live sphagnum
Keep in a tray of rainwater in full sun
Give a cold winter rest outdoors or in a fridge
Don't fertilise; let it catch its own insects

lore: Darwin wrote in 1860 that he cared more for Drosera than for the origin of all the species in the world, and his Insectivorous Plants (1875) begins with it. Italian rosolio liqueur gets its name from the sundew (ros solis, 'dew of the sun').
funFact: A sundew leaf can tell a real insect from a raindrop or grain of sand and responds far more strongly to nitrogen-containing objects.

summary: A tree known only from fossils until 1994, when ranger David Noble abseiled into a gorge in Wollemi National Park near Sydney and found a living grove. Fewer than 100 mature trees survive in the wild, in a location kept secret.
nativeRange: A few sandstone gorges in Wollemi National Park, New South Wales, Australia
abilities: Belongs to an ancient lineage of the Araucariaceae; pollen like it (Dilwynites) goes back about 90 million years
Grows multiple trunks from its base (coppicing), helping it survive rockfall and fire
Sheds whole branches rather than individual leaves
Has bubbly, chocolate-brown bark often compared to the cereal Coco Pops
edibilityNote: Not eaten.

fruit.description: Green spherical female cones at branch tips; male cones lower down.

seed.germination: Sow fresh at 18–25 °C; germination can be patchy

grow.propagation: Cuttings (most plants sold are clones from the 2005 release program)
steps: Buy a nursery-raised plant
Plant in sheltered, well-drained soil or a large pot
Water regularly while young and avoid waterlogging
Never visit the wild site: footsteps carry the deadly Phytophthora cinnamomi root rot

lore: Its 1994 discovery was compared to finding a living dinosaur. In January 2020, during the Black Summer fires, firefighters were winched in by helicopter and set up irrigation and water drops that saved the wild grove.
funFact: Nursery plants were sold worldwide from 2005, partly to remove the incentive for collectors to raid the secret wild grove.

summary: A tree that built empires. Its fragrant, rot-resistant wood went into Phoenician ships, Egyptian tombs and, the Bible says, Solomon's Temple. Ancient demand stripped the Lebanon mountains, so only scattered groves now survive, and the tree stands on the Lebanese flag.
nativeRange: Mountains of Lebanon, western Syria and southern Turkey (Taurus), 1,300–3,000 m
abilities: Grows broad, tiered horizontal branches in old age
Produces aromatic wood rich in sesquiterpenes that resists insects and decay
Lives for well over 1,000 years in favourable sites
Withstands cold, snowy mountain winters and dry Mediterranean summers
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Essential oil is not for internal use.

uses.use: Cedar oil and resin used in embalming (the botanical source of some 'cedar' oils is debated)
Resin and oil applied to skin infections and as an insect repellent

medicinal.cautions: Essential oils can irritate skin and are toxic if swallowed in quantity.

fruit.description: Barrel-shaped cones 8–12 cm that break apart on the tree to release seeds.

seed.description: Resinous seeds with a large wing
seed.germination: Short cold stratification (2–4 weeks); sow in spring

steps: Soak seed overnight and stratify briefly
Sow in deep pots in spring
Plant out young (it dislikes root disturbance) in a spacious, sunny spot
Water through the first summers; after that it is drought-tolerant

lore: In the Epic of Gilgamesh the hero kills Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest, to take its trees. The Cedars of God grove at Bsharri, Lebanon, was inscribed by UNESCO in 1998 with the Qadisha Valley.
funFact: The Palermo Stone records pharaoh Sneferu (c. 2600 BCE) bringing 40 ships filled with cedar wood, usually read as a shipment from Byblos on the Lebanese coast.

summary: A living city. A 2019 study found that English oak supports more than 2,300 species in Britain, including hundreds that live on nothing else. Individual trees can live for more than 1,000 years, and oak has been a sacred tree in Europe since before history.
nativeRange: Most of Europe to the Caucasus and northern Turkey
abilities: Supports more invertebrates, lichens and fungi than any other native British tree
Masts: produces huge acorn crops in some years and few in others, which outpaces seed-eaters
Relies on jays to plant acorns, sometimes kilometres away
Lives for more than 1,000 years, often hollowing out in old age and surviving as a shell
Reacts to gall wasps by growing galls rich in tannin, used for iron-gall ink
edibilityNote: Raw acorns are bitter with tannins and cause stomach upset; they must be leached repeatedly in water before being ground into flour. Acorns and leaves poison cattle and horses in quantity.

uses.use: Bark decoction as an astringent for diarrhoea, sore throats and skin inflammation
Oak bark approved for external use on inflamed skin and for acute diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: High-tannin preparations can irritate the stomach and reduce absorption of other medicines; avoid on large damaged skin areas.

fruit.description: Acorns held in scaly cups on long stalks (peduncles).

seed.description: Acorn; seed must not dry out
seed.dispersal: Jays, squirrels and mice that bury and forget acorns
seed.germination: Sow fresh in autumn; root emerges the same winter, shoot in spring

steps: Collect acorns as they fall and float-test them (discard floaters)
Sow at once in deep pots or straight into the ground
Protect from mice and squirrels with mesh
Plant out within 1–2 years before the taproot gets long

lore: Pliny the Elder described Gaulish druids cutting mistletoe from oaks with a golden sickle, and Charles II hid in the 'Royal Oak' at Boscobel in 1651. Oak was the timber of the Royal Navy and of Europe's cathedrals.
funFact: Magna Carta, Leonardo's notebooks and Bach's manuscripts were written in iron-gall ink, made from tannin-rich oak galls and iron salts.

summary: The tree that shades out nearly everything else. Beech casts such deep shade that it came to dominate huge areas of Europe after the last Ice Age, forming cathedral-like forests with almost no undergrowth. The word 'book' comes from it.
nativeRange: Western, central and southern Europe, from southern Scandinavia to Sicily and the Balkans
abilities: Casts some of the deepest shade of any European tree, suppressing competitors
Its seedlings tolerate deep shade for decades, waiting for a gap to open
Masts heavily every few years, flooding the forest with beechnuts
Forms extensive root networks with ectomycorrhizal fungi such as chanterelles and ceps
edibilityNote: Beechnuts are edible in small amounts and better roasted; eating many raw causes stomach upset, from mildly toxic compounds (historically called "fagin"). Beechnuts are toxic to horses.

fruit.description: Bristly husks that split into four to release two triangular nuts.

seed.dispersal: Gravity, plus jays, rodents and formerly pigs
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 8–12 weeks; sow in spring

steps: Collect nuts as they fall and stratify over winter
Sow in spring in pots or a seedbed
Keep young plants lightly shaded and moist
Plant as a tree or keep clipped as a hedge, which holds brown leaves all winter

lore: Germanic peoples carved runes on beech tablets, and the Old English 'bōc' and German 'Buche/Buch' link beech and book. The 'Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe' became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007 and later grew to cover 18 countries.
funFact: Beech holds dead leaves through winter when kept as a young tree or hedge (marcescence), which is why beech hedges stay brown and dense in winter.

summary: The pioneer of the north. Silver birch is among the first trees to recolonise burned, cleared or glacier-scoured ground, and its white bark, rich in betulin, reflects sunlight. People have tapped its sap, written on its bark and built canoes and boxes from it for thousands of years.
nativeRange: Most of Europe to Siberia and northern Kazakhstan, south to Turkey and Iran
abilities: Disperses millions of light winged seeds, so it is quick to colonise open ground
Its bark is rich in betulin, a white triterpene that reflects light and repels water
Pushes large volumes of sugary sap up in spring before leafing out
Prepares soil for later trees by cycling nutrients through fast-rotting leaves
edibilityNote: Sap is drunk fresh in spring across Eastern Europe and Scandinavia. Birch pollen is a major cause of hay fever, and people with birch allergy often react to raw apples, hazelnuts and cherries.

uses.use: Leaf tea as a diuretic for urinary tract irrigation (approved by German Commission E)
Birch tar (dyogot) applied to skin conditions; birch twigs used in the banya

medicinal.cautions: Not for people with oedema from heart or kidney failure. Birch tar contains irritants. Birch pollen allergy is common.

fruit.description: Cylindrical catkins break up into tiny winged seeds and three-lobed scales.

seed.germination: Surface-sow; needs light. Brief cold stratification improves germination.

grow.timeToHarvest: Sap from trees ~20 cm diameter, about 15–20 years
steps: Surface-sow seed in late winter and keep moist and bright
Plant out small: birches transplant poorly when larger
To tap sap, drill a small hole in early spring before bud-break and collect for a few days only
Plug the tap hole afterwards to protect the tree

lore: Medieval citizens of Novgorod scratched letters onto birch bark; more than 1,000 such 'beresty' documents have been dug up since 1951. Ötzi the Iceman carried birch-bark containers and birch-tar adhesive. It is the national tree of Finland and Russia.
funFact: Birch tar is the oldest known synthetic material; Neanderthals were making it as a glue more than 200,000 years ago.

summary: The source of maple syrup and the blaze of New England autumns. On spring days after freezing nights, pressure changes inside the wood push sugary sap out of any wound, and about 40 litres of sap boil down to one litre of syrup.
nativeRange: Eastern Canada and north-eastern and central United States
abilities: Flows sap during freeze–thaw cycles, when gas pressure in the wood fibres pushes sap from wounds
Lifts water from deep soil at night and releases it into dry topsoil (hydraulic lift), which helps nearby plants
Turns brilliant red, orange and yellow in autumn as chlorophyll breaks down and anthocyanins form
Tolerates deep shade as a sapling, waiting decades for a canopy gap
edibilityNote: Sap is boiled into syrup and sugar. Not toxic to people, but wilted leaves of the related red maple (Acer rubrum) poison horses.

fruit.description: Paired winged seeds ('helicopters') joined at a U-shaped angle.

seed.description: Round seed at the base of a papery wing
seed.germination: Cold-stratify 60–90 days; sow in spring

grow.soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained; dislikes road salt
grow.timeToHarvest: Tap for syrup at about 25 cm diameter (30–40 years)
steps: Stratify seed over winter in moist sand
Sow in spring; protect seedlings from deer
Plant in deep, moist, well-drained soil away from salted roads
Tap in late winter when days are above freezing and nights below; boil the sap down to 66% sugar

lore: Anishinaabe, Haudenosaunee and other nations made maple sugar long before Europeans arrived, holding sugar camps each spring; the Haudenosaunee honour the sap run with a Maple Ceremony of thanksgiving. A stylised maple leaf has been on Canada's flag since 1965.
funFact: The 2012 'Great Canadian Maple Syrup Heist' saw about 3,000 tonnes of syrup, worth around C$18 million, stolen from a Quebec strategic reserve.

summary: A tree in the mint family that became the world's most famous ship timber. Teak's oily, silica-rich wood shrugs off water, rot and termites, so it was used for warships, temples and deck planks for centuries. The great natural teak forests of Myanmar, Laos and Thailand are now largely gone.
nativeRange: India, Myanmar, Laos and Thailand; long naturalised in Java; plantations across the tropics
abilities: Makes heartwood with natural oils and tectoquinone that repel termites and fungi
Its wood barely shrinks or swells with moisture, so it was ideal for ship decks
Drops its huge leaves in the dry season and survives fire
Its leaves are among the largest of any tree, up to about 50 cm long, and yield a red dye
edibilityNote: Not a food. Leaves are used to wrap food in parts of India and Java. Teak sawdust can cause dermatitis and asthma.

uses.use: Bark and wood (shaka) as astringent; leaf preparations for skin disease and bleeding
Young leaves used as a red dye and for skin problems

medicinal.cautions: Teak dust is a skin and respiratory sensitiser for woodworkers.

fruit.description: Hard, four-chambered stone inside a papery, balloon-like calyx.

seed.description: Very hard, woody fruit stone with up to four seeds
seed.germination: Alternately soak and sun-dry fruits for 1–2 weeks to break dormancy; germination is erratic

steps: Soak fruits overnight and sun-dry by day for 1–2 weeks
Sow in nursery beds; transplant 'stumps' (pruned seedlings) at the start of the rains
Weed well: teak is intolerant of competition
Thin plantings over time to produce straight trunks

lore: Britain's Royal Navy and the East India Company built ships from Malabar and Burmese teak, and the timber trade shaped colonial forestry in British India.
funFact: Teak is in the mint family, Lamiaceae, the same family as basil and lavender.

summary: The 'true' mahogany of fine furniture, whose deep-red, stable wood made it one of the most valuable timbers of the Americas. Heavy logging ran ahead of the law, and it was listed on CITES Appendix II in 2003. Its fruit capsules point skyward and split open to release winged seeds.
nativeRange: Southern Mexico through Central America to the Amazon basin (Bolivia, Brazil, Peru)
abilities: Produces dense, stable, rot-resistant red-brown heartwood
Its upright capsules split into five valves and release winged seeds that spin away on the wind
Grows into a forest giant over 40 m tall with buttressed trunks
Regenerates best after large disturbances such as floods, fires or hurricanes
edibilityNote: Not a food. Seeds are very bitter and used only medicinally; high doses have been linked to liver injury.

uses.use: Seeds taken for diabetes and high blood pressure
Bark decoctions for fever and diarrhoea

medicinal.cautions: Seed preparations have caused liver toxicity in case reports; they may add to the effect of diabetes drugs.

fruit.description: Upright, pear-shaped brown capsules 12–20 cm long that split from the base.

seed.description: Flat seeds with a long brown wing
seed.germination: Sow fresh (short viability); 2–4 weeks in warmth

steps: Sow fresh seed with the wing pointing up, barely covered
Keep in partial shade in the nursery
Plant out in mixed stands: monocultures are attacked by the mahogany shoot borer (Hypsipyla)
Prune to a single leader

lore: Mahogany furniture became a status symbol in 18th-century Britain, and Chippendale's designs relied on Caribbean and Central American mahogany cut and shipped largely by enslaved and forced labour. Illegal logging of mogno in the Brazilian Amazon was a major conservation scandal of the 1990s.
funFact: In Malaysia the seed is called 'sky fruit' because its capsules point straight up at the sky.

summary: A tree that walks into the sea on stilts. Red mangroves arch prop roots into salty mud, keep most of the salt out at the root surface, and drop seedlings that have already germinated on the tree and can float for months. Their roots shelter young fish and buffer coasts from storms.
nativeRange: Tropical Atlantic and eastern Pacific coasts: Florida, Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Central and South America, West Africa; introduced to Hawaii
abilities: Is viviparous: seeds germinate on the tree and drop as pencil-like propagules up to about 30 cm long
Its propagules float and stay viable for months, colonising new coasts
Its roots filter out most salt from seawater
Breathes through lenticels on prop roots that stand above the anoxic mud
Builds coastlines by trapping sediment and buffers storm surge
edibilityNote: Propagules have been eaten as famine food after processing, but they are astringent and bitter; generally not eaten.

uses.tradition: Caribbean and Latin American folk medicine
uses.use: Bark decoction as an astringent for diarrhoea, sore throat and wounds

medicinal.cautions: High-tannin preparations can irritate the gut.

fruit.season: Much of the year, peaking in summer
fruit.description: Brown leathery fruit from which a long green propagule grows while still on the tree.

seed.description: Germinates on the tree into a long, cigar-shaped propagule
seed.germination: Already germinated; plant the propagule upright in tidal mud

lore: The word 'mangle' came into Spanish from the Taíno of the Caribbean. Tannin from red mangrove bark was used across the tropics to tan leather and preserve fishing nets and sails, giving them a red-brown colour.
funFact: Mangrove propagules can drift for months and still root, which is how Rhizophora reached both sides of the Atlantic.

summary: A moss that builds landscapes and stores carbon. Sphagnum holds many times its own weight in water in dead, empty cells, acidifies its surroundings, and decays so slowly that its remains pile up as peat. Peatlands cover about 3% of Earth's land but store more carbon than all the world's forests combined.
nativeRange: Widespread in temperate and boreal regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with records from other continents
abilities: Holds up to around 20 times its dry weight in water in large, dead hyaline cells
Acidifies its environment by exchanging hydrogen ions for mineral cations
Builds peat that preserves organic matter for thousands of years, including bog bodies such as Tollund Man
Fires its spores out of a pressurised capsule, forming a tiny vortex ring that carries them upward
edibilityNote: Not eaten.

uses.use: Dried sphagnum used as absorbent, mildly antiseptic wound dressings by the million

uses.tradition: Northern Indigenous and European folk practice
uses.use: Used as nappy lining and menstrual padding

medicinal.cautions: Sphagnum can carry the fungus Sporothrix, which causes 'rose gardener's disease' through skin cuts; wear gloves.

seed.description: Spores in a round capsule on a short stalk
seed.germination: Mostly spreads from fragments; place live strands on wet peat

grow.timeToHarvest: Covers a tray in a few months
steps: Spread chopped live strands on wet peat in a tray
Keep wet with rainwater and humid
Give bright light to keep it compact and colourful
Use it as a living top-dressing for carnivorous plants

lore: Bog acids and sphagnan in Sphagnum peat preserved Iron Age bodies such as Tollund Man (found in Denmark in 1950) in astonishing detail. Peat cut from sphagnum bogs fuelled homes in Ireland, Scotland and the Netherlands for centuries.
funFact: High-speed video shows Sphagnum capsules launching spores at about 3.6 m/s, with the spores lifted 10–20 cm by a self-made vortex ring.

summary: One of the fastest-growing organisms on Earth, adding up to about half a metre a day and reaching lengths of 45 m or more. Giant kelp is a brown alga, not a plant, and forms underwater forests that shelter fish, sea otters and countless invertebrates.
nativeRange: Cool coastal waters of the eastern Pacific (Alaska to Baja California; Peru and Chile), the southern Atlantic and sub-Antarctic coasts, southern Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Grows up to about 50 cm a day in good conditions
Floats its fronds to the surface with gas-filled bladders (pneumatocysts) at each blade
Grips rock with a root-like holdfast that is not used for feeding
Builds forest habitats that support hundreds of species, kept in balance by sea otters that eat kelp-grazing urchins
edibilityNote: Edible, but very high in iodine; frequent large servings can upset thyroid function. Can concentrate heavy metals such as arsenic from polluted water.

seed.description: Reproduces by microscopic zoospores released from special blades (sporophylls) near the base
seed.dispersal: Water currents, mostly over short distances
seed.germination: Spores grow into tiny male and female gametophytes whose offspring become new kelp

lore: The 'kelp highway' hypothesis proposes that early people followed productive kelp-forest coasts around the Pacific Rim into the Americas. Darwin, on the Beagle, compared southern kelp forests to land forests and said their loss would destroy many animals.
funFact: For much of the 20th century, giant kelp harvested off California was a major source of alginate, the thickener in ice cream, toothpaste and wound dressings.

summary: A grass that grows into a forest. Moso shoots can push up close to a metre a day and reach full height of 20 m or more in a couple of months. It is China's most important timber bamboo, used for scaffolding, flooring, textiles and the spring shoots of East Asian cooking.
nativeRange: Central and southern China and Taiwan; long cultivated in Japan
abilities: New culms can grow close to 1 m in a day at peak growth
A culm reaches full height in one season and then hardens for several years
Spreads by vigorous running rhizomes, forming huge connected groves
Flowers only at long intervals; a Japanese stand flowered 67 years after sowing, then died
edibilityNote: Shoots must be peeled and boiled before eating: raw shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides (taxiphyllin) that release cyanide.

fruit.description: Grass-like grains produced only in rare flowering events.

seed.germination: Sow fresh at 20–25 °C; viability drops within months

grow.timeToHarvest: Shoots in spring after 3–5 years; timber culms at 4–6 years
steps: Plant a rhizome division in spring in deep, rich soil
Install a rhizome barrier at least 60 cm deep, since running bamboo invades
Water and mulch heavily
Harvest shoots as they emerge in spring and boil them before eating

lore: Chinese literati such as Su Shi praised bamboo, and moso is part of the story of Meng Zong, one of the Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars, who wept in a winter grove until bamboo shoots sprang up for his sick mother; the Japanese name 'mōsōchiku' honours him.
funFact: A moso grove is often a single connected plant, with every culm linked by an underground rhizome network.

summary: The flower that rises clean from the mud, central to Hinduism and Buddhism. Its leaves are so water-repellent that droplets roll off carrying dirt with them (the 'lotus effect'), its flowers warm themselves, and a seed about 1,300 years old has been sprouted.
nativeRange: South and East Asia to northern Australia; ancient introductions elsewhere
abilities: Its leaf surface is covered in wax nano-bumps that make it superhydrophobic and self-cleaning
Warms its flowers to around 30–35 °C for days, even on cool nights
Produces seeds that can stay alive for centuries; one from a dry lakebed in north-east China germinated after about 1,300 years
Pipes air down to its rhizomes through hollow channels in its stalks
edibilityNote: All main parts are eaten. Cook the rhizome before eating, since raw aquatic plants can carry parasites such as Fasciolopsis; remove the bitter green embryo of seeds if desired.

uses.use: Seeds (lian zi) to calm the heart; leaves (he ye) for summer heat; the seed embryo (lian zi xin) as a cooling bitter
Flowers and rhizome (kamala) for bleeding, diarrhoea and skin conditions

medicinal.cautions: Leaf and embryo preparations may lower blood pressure and blood sugar; caution with medication.

fruit.description: A flat-topped, shower-head seed pod with each nut set in its own hole.

seed.dispersal: Water, after the pod tips over
seed.germination: File through the hard coat at the non-pointed end and soak in warm water; sprouts in days

grow.soil: Heavy loam or clay at the pond bottom
grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers in 1–2 years from seed; rhizomes after one season
steps: Nick the seed coat and soak in warm water, changing it daily
Pot the sprouted seed into heavy loam in a wide, hole-free container
Submerge in still, sunny water and raise depth as leaves grow
Give at least 6 hours of sun and warm water to flower

lore: In Hindu iconography Lakshmi and Brahma sit on lotuses, and Buddhist art shows the Buddha on a lotus throne; 'Om mani padme hum' means 'the jewel in the lotus'. Zhou Dunyi's 11th-century essay 'On the Love of the Lotus' praised it for rising unstained from mud.
funFact: Self-cleaning paints and fabrics are modelled on the lotus leaf's microstructure; 'lotus effect' is a registered trademark.

summary: A water lily whose leaves reach up to about 3 m across, ribbed underneath like the girders of a bridge. Its flowers open white and fragrant on the first night, shut beetles inside, and reopen pink the next night to release them covered in pollen.
nativeRange: Amazon basin: Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, Guyana
abilities: Grows floating leaves up to about 3 m across with upturned rims
Its spiny underside ribs trap air and spread load, so a leaf can bear a small child if weight is spread
Heats its first-night flower and releases a pineapple-like scent to attract Cyclocephala scarab beetles
Changes sex in two nights: female and white on night one, male and pink on night two
edibilityNote: Starchy seeds are roasted or ground into flour locally. Stalks and leaf undersides are covered in sharp spines.

fruit.description: Prickly fruit that develops underwater and releases pea-sized seeds.

seed.germination: Store in water (they die if dried); germinate at about 30 °C

grow.zones: Tropical only (USDA 11–12) or heated glasshouse pool
grow.soil: Rich, heavy loam in a large container
steps: Keep seed in water until sowing
Germinate in shallow water at about 30 °C
Move to a large, very fertile container in a big warm pool
Fertilise heavily: a single plant needs a lot of feeding

lore: John Lindley named the genus after the young Queen Victoria in 1837 from specimens Robert Schomburgk sent from British Guiana; Joseph Paxton at Chatsworth first brought it to flower in November 1849. Paxton said the ribbed leaf inspired the iron-and-glass structure of the Crystal Palace for the Great Exhibition of 1851.
funFact: Paxton had his daughter Annie stand on a leaf (on a tray to spread her weight), an image that made the plant famous.

summary: The giant cactus of the Sonoran Desert, which can grow taller than 12 m, live for around 150–200 years and weigh several tonnes when full of water. It may take 50–100 years to grow its first arm. Its pleats swell like an accordion after rain.
nativeRange: Sonoran Desert of Arizona, south-eastern California and Sonora, Mexico
abilities: Expands its pleated stem to store hundreds of litres of water after rain
Opens night-blooming flowers pollinated by lesser long-nosed bats, then birds and bees by day
Its hollows, carved by Gila woodpeckers and gilded flickers, house owls, martins and other birds
Feeds desert animals in early summer, when its fruit ripens and little else is available
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten fresh, dried, or boiled into syrup and jam. Harvesting from wild plants on protected land requires permission.

fruit.description: Green fruits split to reveal red pulp packed with tiny black seeds.

seed.germination: Surface-sow on gritty mix, warm and humid; seedlings need shade

steps: Surface-sow seed under a clear cover and keep warm and lightly moist
Shade seedlings, as wild ones grow under 'nurse' trees like palo verde
Water sparingly; protect from frost
Buy only nursery-grown plants: removing wild saguaros is illegal in Arizona

lore: For the Tohono O'odham the saguaro harvest (bahidaj) in early summer begins the new year, and fermented saguaro wine is used in a rain ceremony to call the monsoon. The saguaro blossom is Arizona's state flower.
funFact: Saguaro seedlings may grow only a few centimetres in their first decade.

summary: The shaggy, twisted tree-yucca of the Mojave Desert, which depends completely on one moth. The yucca moth deliberately packs pollen into the flower and lays its eggs there, and its larvae eat some, but not all, of the seeds. Climate warming is shrinking the areas where it can live.
nativeRange: Western Mojave Desert, California and Nevada (eastern populations often treated as Yucca jaegeriana)
abilities: Is pollinated only by the yucca moth Tegeticula synthetica, which gathers pollen and stuffs it into the flower on purpose
Sprouts clones from roots and rhizomes, especially after damage
Branches only after flowering or when the growing tip is damaged
Provides nest sites and food for desert birds, lizards and woodrats
edibilityNote: Indigenous peoples of the Mojave roasted the buds and ate the seeds. Like other yuccas it contains saponins, which are bitter and can upset the stomach.

fruit.description: Green, egg-shaped capsules that dry and release flat black seeds.

seed.germination: Sow fresh, warm, in sandy mix; germination is quick but seedlings are slow

steps: Sow seed in deep pots of sandy mix
Keep warm and barely moist
Plant out young in full sun on free-draining ground
Do not move wild plants: Joshua trees are protected in California

lore: Mormon settlers crossing the Mojave in the 1850s are said to have named it after the biblical Joshua, raising his hands to heaven. The Cahuilla used its leaf fibres for baskets and sandals and its roots for red dye.
funFact: Studies predict that under high-warming scenarios Joshua Tree National Park could lose most of its suitable Joshua tree habitat by 2100.

summary: One aspen grove in Utah, called Pando, is a single male clone with about 47,000 trunks on one root system, covering some 43 hectares and weighing around 6,000 tonnes. It is often called the heaviest known organism. Aspen leaves flutter in the faintest breeze on flattened stalks.
nativeRange: Across Canada and Alaska, south through the Rocky Mountains to northern Mexico
abilities: Spreads by root suckers into vast clones; Pando is one genetic individual of about 47,000 stems
Its flattened leaf stalks make leaves tremble in the slightest wind
Photosynthesises through its pale green-white bark, even in winter
Re-sprouts quickly after fire, acting as a natural firebreak and pioneer
Is the most widely distributed tree in North America
edibilityNote: Inner bark was eaten in spring by Indigenous peoples and in hard times. Bark contains salicin and related compounds, so people with aspirin allergy should avoid it.

uses.use: Bark tea for fever, pain and coughs; the bark's white powder used as sunscreen

medicinal.cautions: Salicylates: avoid with aspirin allergy, anticoagulants, and in children with viral illness.

fruit.description: Catkins of small capsules that release cottony seeds.

seed.germination: Sow immediately on moist soil; viability lasts only days to weeks

grow.propagation: Root cuttings or suckers; fresh seed
grow.timeToHarvest: Ornamental; individual stems live about 100–150 years
steps: Take root cuttings or dig a sucker in early spring
Plant in full sun with space to spread
Expect suckers; mow or cut them where unwanted
Protect young stems from deer and elk browsing

lore: Pando was identified as one clone in the 1970s, and genetic testing in 2008 confirmed it. A 2024 genetic study estimated Pando may be between about 16,000 and 80,000 years old, though this is uncertain.
funFact: Pando is not regenerating well, because mule deer and elk eat nearly all young shoots; fenced areas are being used to help it.

summary: A plant that folds its leaves within seconds when touched. Electrical signals travel through the stem, and motor cells in swellings at the leaf bases suddenly lose water and collapse. Experiments suggest it can 'learn' to ignore harmless repeated disturbances.
nativeRange: Tropical Central and South America; now a pantropical weed
abilities: Folds leaflets within seconds of touch, heat or shaking (seismonasty) using pulvinus motor cells
Sends electrical action potentials along its stem to coordinate leaf collapse
Folds its leaves at night on an internal circadian clock
In a 2014 experiment, stopped folding in response to repeated harmless drops and kept this 'memory' for weeks
Fixes nitrogen through root nodules
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Contains the amino acid mimosine, toxic to livestock in quantity (hair loss, poor growth). Stems carry small prickles.

uses.use: Roots and leaves (lajjalu) for bleeding piles, diarrhoea and wound healing

uses.tradition: Traditional medicine in the Philippines and Africa
uses.use: Leaf poultices for wounds and swellings

medicinal.cautions: Mimosine is toxic in large amounts; avoid in pregnancy. Invasive weed in many countries.

fruit.season: Most of the year in the tropics
fruit.description: Clusters of small, bristly pods that break into one-seeded segments.

seed.dispersal: Pod segments stick to fur and clothing
seed.germination: Soak in hot water overnight; sow at 20–30 °C, 1–3 weeks

grow.timeToHarvest: Responsive leaves in a few weeks
steps: Pour hot water over seeds and soak overnight
Sow shallowly in warm, bright conditions
Keep evenly moist and above 15 °C
Grow in a pot where it is invasive outdoors

lore: In 1729 French astronomer Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Mairan kept a sensitive plant in total darkness and found its leaves still opened and closed daily, the first experiment showing an internal biological clock.
funFact: Monica Gagliano's 2014 experiment found habituated plants still 'remembered' to ignore harmless drops up to 28 days later.

summary: A plant disguised as a pebble. Each Lithops is just a pair of fat, fused leaves sunk in the ground, with only patterned 'windows' at the top showing. Light enters through these windows and lights up the inside of the leaf, letting it photosynthesise while staying mostly buried.
nativeRange: Grasslands and rocky outcrops of northern South Africa (Gauteng, North West, Free State, Limpopo, Northern Cape) and edges of Botswana
abilities: Camouflages as stones, with colours that match the local rock
Lets light into the leaf through translucent 'windows' on top while the rest of the body stays below ground
Each year grows a new pair of leaves inside the old, which then shrivels and is absorbed
Its seed capsules open only when wet, so raindrops splash seeds out
edibilityNote: Not eaten.

fruit.description: Small capsules that open when wet and close as they dry.

seed.germination: Surface-sow on gritty mix, keep humid at 15–25 °C; 1–3 weeks

grow.sun: Full sun to very bright light
grow.water: Very low; water in summer and autumn growth, none while old leaves are being absorbed
grow.soil: Mostly mineral grit (pumice, sand) with a little compost
steps: Surface-sow seed on fine grit and cover to hold humidity
Gradually reduce humidity as seedlings grow
Water during summer–autumn growth; stop while new leaves are emerging
Overwatering is the main cause of death: the old leaves split and rot

lore: Named after Thomas Leslie, an amateur botanist who collected it near Pietersburg (now Polokwane) in 1912. Afrikaans farmers called Lithops 'beeskloutjies' because their split shape looks like a cow's hoof print.
funFact: Lithops are so well hidden that many species were found only when the plants were flowering.

summary: A desert spikemoss that can dry out until it looks dead, curl into a tight brown ball, and turn green again within hours of being watered. It can lose about 95% of its water and survive for years like this. It belongs to the lycophytes, a lineage more than 400 million years old.
nativeRange: Chihuahuan Desert of northern Mexico and south-western United States (Texas, New Mexico, Arizona)
abilities: Survives losing about 95% of its water content (desiccation tolerance)
Curls its stems inward as it dries, protecting the living centre from sun
Accumulates trehalose and other sugars that protect its cells while dry
Uncurls and resumes photosynthesis within hours of rehydrating
edibilityNote: Not a food; used only as a tea in folk medicine.

uses.use: Tea (doradilla) for kidney stones, urinary complaints and as a diuretic

medicinal.cautions: Little safety data; avoid in pregnancy.

seed.description: Reproduces by spores (no seeds): large megaspores and tiny microspores
seed.dispersal: Wind and water; also tumbles when uprooted
seed.germination: Usually grown from divisions rather than spores

steps: Set the dry ball on a dish of gravel with a little water
Let it open and green up, then move it onto gritty soil
Allow it to dry out between waterings; constant wet causes rot
It can be dried and revived repeatedly, but each cycle stresses it

lore: Sold in Mexican and US markets for luck and prosperity, often under the name 'rose of Jericho', a name that belongs to the Middle Eastern Anastatica hierochuntica. In Mexican tradition it is placed in water on Fridays to bring good fortune.
funFact: It is not a moss and not a fern, but a lycophyte, related to the giant club-mosses whose remains formed much of the world's coal.

summary: A tree armoured with dark conical spikes whose pumpkin-shaped seed capsules explode with a sound like a gunshot. Recorded seed speeds reach about 70 m/s, throwing seeds tens of metres. Its milky sap is caustic and has been used as fish poison and arrow poison.
nativeRange: Tropical Americas, from Central America and the Caribbean to the Amazon; invasive in parts of tropical Africa
abilities: Its drying capsules build tension and burst apart, launching seeds at around 60–70 m/s
Throws seeds up to about 45 m from the tree
Protects its trunk with dense, sharp conical spines
Grows fast into a canopy tree up to 40–60 m
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic. The milky sap (latex) causes blistering skin burns and can cause serious eye damage. Seeds cause violent vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea if eaten; they contain the toxic protein hurin. Children are sometimes poisoned after eating the seeds, which resemble small nuts.

fruit.description: Segmented capsules like small pumpkins, up to 8 cm across, that dry and explode.

seed.germination: Sow fresh in warm soil; handle with gloves

lore: Before blotting paper, the unripe capsules were cut and filled with fine sand used to blot ink, the origin of the name 'sandbox'. Carib peoples reportedly used the sap to poison arrows and stun fish.
funFact: The species name crepitans means 'crackling' in Latin, for the gunshot crack of its exploding capsules.

summary: One of humanity's oldest crops, grown for rope and cloth, edible seeds, oil, medicine and its mind-altering resin. The flowers' resin glands make THC and CBD, compounds that act on the body's own endocannabinoid system.
nativeRange: Central and South Asia (possibly East Asia); cultivated worldwide
abilities: Produces long, strong bast fibres used for rope, sails, paper and cloth
Makes resin in glandular trichomes rich in cannabinoids (THC, CBD) and terpenes
Many varieties switch to flowering when nights lengthen
Grows extremely fast, reaching 2–5 m in one season
edibilityNote: Hemp seeds and oil contain little or no THC and are widely eaten. Flowers and resin are psychoactive; edibles can cause severe intoxication, especially in children and pets (dogs are very sensitive). Legal status varies by country.

uses.use: Purified bhang (vijaya) for pain, digestion and sleep
Seeds (huo ma ren) as a laxative
Purified CBD (Epidiolex) approved for certain epilepsies; THC drugs (dronabinol, nabilone) for chemotherapy nausea and appetite loss

medicinal.cautions: THC can cause anxiety, psychosis in vulnerable people, impaired driving and dependence; heavy use is linked to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome. CBD interacts with drugs such as clobazam and blood thinners. Avoid in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Small, smooth, grey-brown seeds enclosed in a bract.

seed.germination: Sow 1 cm deep at 20–25 °C; 3–7 days

steps: Check local laws: growing is restricted or licensed in many places
Sow after the last frost in fertile soil
For fibre, sow densely; for seed, sow widely spaced
Harvest fibre stems at early flowering; harvest seed when most seeds are brown

lore: Hemp cloth and cord are known from Neolithic China, and Herodotus (5th century BCE) described Scythians throwing hemp seeds on hot stones and howling with joy in the vapour. Braziers from a ~2,500-year-old cemetery at Jirzankal in the Pamirs contain residues of high-THC cannabis.
funFact: The English word 'canvas' comes from cannabis, via Old French and Latin.

summary: The sacred leaf of the Andes, chewed for thousands of years to ease hunger, fatigue and altitude. Its leaves contain about 0.5–1% cocaine, which in the leaf form is mild, but became a powerful drug of addiction once it was extracted in 1860.
nativeRange: Eastern slopes of the Andes in Peru and Bolivia; cultivated in Colombia and elsewhere
abilities: Makes cocaine and related alkaloids in its leaves, which deter insect herbivores
Grows on steep, terraced Andean slopes and can be harvested several times a year
Its leaf is nutritious, with significant calcium and iron
edibilityNote: Leaves are chewed with an alkaline ash (llipta) or brewed as mate de coca, legal in Peru and Bolivia but illegal in many countries. Extracted cocaine is highly addictive and can cause heart attack, stroke and death. Leaf use causes positive drug tests.

uses.use: Leaves chewed or drunk as tea for altitude sickness, hunger, fatigue and stomach pain
Cocaine hydrochloride used as a topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor in nose and throat procedures

medicinal.cautions: Cocaine is addictive and cardiotoxic. Leaf products are controlled in most countries outside the Andes.

fruit.description: Small red drupes about 1 cm long.

seed.germination: Sow fresh; germinates in a few weeks

lore: Coca appears in Moche ceramics showing chewers with bulging cheeks, and under the Inca its use was reserved largely for nobility and ritual. Albert Niemann isolated cocaine in 1860, and in 1884 Carl Koller showed it could numb the eye for surgery, the first local anaesthetic.
funFact: Coca-Cola originally contained coca extract; the company still uses de-cocainised coca leaf flavouring, processed by a single licensed US facility.

summary: A small spineless cactus of the Chihuahuan Desert that produces mescaline, used in ceremony by Indigenous peoples for at least 5,700 years. It grows very slowly, taking years to reach harvest size, and overharvesting and land clearing have made it vulnerable.
nativeRange: Chihuahuan Desert and Tamaulipan thornscrub of southern Texas and north-central Mexico
abilities: Synthesises mescaline and dozens of related phenethylamine and isoquinoline alkaloids
Has no spines; relies on bitter alkaloids and camouflage under shrubs
Regrows new 'buttons' from its carrot-like root after the crown is cut, if cut correctly
Grows extremely slowly, often 10+ years to flowering size in the wild
edibilityNote: Not a food. The crown is intensely bitter and typically causes nausea and vomiting, along with powerful hallucinations from mescaline, raised heart rate and blood pressure. Dangerous for people with heart conditions or psychosis; illegal in most places except for protected religious use.

uses.tradition: Indigenous Mexican and Native American medicine
uses.use: Used for pain, fever, wounds and in healing ceremonies
Sacramental use in all-night prayer meetings

medicinal.cautions: Hallucinogenic; can trigger psychosis and dangerous behaviour; interacts with MAOIs and other drugs.

fruit.description: Small, pink, club-shaped fruit with black seeds.

seed.germination: Surface-sow on gritty mix under cover; very slow growth

lore: Peyote buttons found in Shumla Caves, Texas, have been radiocarbon-dated to about 5,700 years ago. The Wixárika (Huichol) make an annual pilgrimage to Wirikuta in San Luis Potosí to gather hikuri, and US federal law (AIRFA amendments, 1994) protects its sacramental use by Native American Church members.
funFact: Mescaline, isolated from peyote by Arthur Heffter in 1897, was the first psychedelic compound ever isolated.

summary: A woody Amazonian liana at the heart of ayahuasca, the visionary brew of many Amazonian peoples. Its harmala alkaloids block the enzyme monoamine oxidase, which lets DMT from leaves such as chacruna (Psychotria viridis) act when drunk.
nativeRange: Amazon basin and adjacent tropical South America (Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia)
abilities: Makes β-carboline alkaloids (harmine, harmaline, tetrahydroharmine) that inhibit monoamine oxidase A
Climbs high into the rainforest canopy as a thick, twisting liana
Its MAO inhibition allows DMT to be orally active, a combination Indigenous peoples discovered without any chemistry
edibilityNote: Not a food. The brew causes vomiting and diarrhoea (regarded as 'purging' in ritual) and intense visions. Dangerous with SSRIs, other antidepressants, stimulants and certain foods because MAO inhibition can cause serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis; deaths have occurred, often with mixed brews or drug interactions.

uses.use: Healing, divination and spiritual guidance in ceremonies led by curanderos

uses.tradition: Brazilian ayahuasca religions (Santo Daime, União do Vegetal)
uses.use: Sacramental use
Small trials of ayahuasca for treatment-resistant depression

medicinal.cautions: MAO inhibitor: serious interactions with antidepressants, stimulants and tyramine-rich foods; not for people with psychosis, heart disease or in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Winged fruits typical of the Malpighia family.

seed.germination: Usually propagated by stem cuttings rather than seed

lore: English botanist Richard Spruce collected the vine among the Tukanoan peoples of the Rio Negro in 1851. In 2006 the US Supreme Court (Gonzales v. O Centro Espírita Beneficente União do Vegetal) upheld a church's right to use hoasca tea.
funFact: Harmine was once called 'telepathine' in the 1920s because of the visions reported by those who drank ayahuasca.

summary: A beautiful, tough flowering shrub planted on highways and in gardens throughout warm climates, and one of the most poisonous common garden plants. Every part contains cardiac glycosides that disrupt the heart's rhythm. It was the first plant to bloom in Hiroshima after the 1945 bombing.
nativeRange: Mediterranean region and North Africa through the Middle East to South Asia and southern China
abilities: Tolerates drought, salt spray, heat, poor soil and city pollution
Makes potent cardiac glycosides (oleandrin) in all its tissues
Grows along seasonal riverbeds, surviving floods and long dry seasons
Its flowers offer no nectar; it is pollinated by insects that it 'deceives'
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous: leaves, flowers, stems, seeds, roots and sap, fresh or dried. The cardiac glycosides oleandrin and neriine cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, slow or irregular heartbeat, high blood potassium and can cause fatal cardiac arrest. Smoke from burning it, using stems as skewers, and honey from oleander-rich areas have all caused poisoning. Deadly to dogs, cats, horses and livestock. Treatment may include digoxin-specific antibody fragments. Not to be confused with yellow oleander (Cascabela thevetia), also deadly.

uses.use: Root and leaf (karavira), after purification, applied externally for skin diseases
Leaf preparations used externally for ringworm and swelling

medicinal.cautions: Potentially fatal if taken internally; 'oleandrin' supplements and extracts are dangerous and unproven.

fruit.description: Long, narrow paired pods that split to release silky-haired seeds.

seed.description: Brown seeds with a tuft of hairs
seed.germination: Usually propagated by cuttings; seed germinates readily in warmth

steps: Wear gloves when pruning; the sap irritates skin
Root cuttings in water or moist sand in summer
Plant in full sun away from where children and pets play
Never burn the prunings or use stems as skewers

lore: Oleander is painted in the garden frescoes of Pompeii, and Pliny the Elder warned that it was poisonous to animals. Oleander is the official flower of Hiroshima because it was the first to bloom after the atomic bombing.
funFact: Despite its poison, oleander is the main food of the oleander caterpillar (larva of the polka-dot wasp moth, Syntomeida epilais), which stores the plant's toxins for its own defence.

summary: A fast-growing, dramatic plant whose mottled seeds hold both castor oil and ricin, one of the most toxic natural proteins. Pressing separates them: the oil is a safe, ancient laxative and industrial lubricant, while ricin stays in the seed cake.
nativeRange: Probably north-eastern Africa (Ethiopia) and the Middle East; naturalised throughout the tropics and warm temperate regions
abilities: Produces ricin, a protein that disables ribosomes and stops cells making proteins
Stores up to ~50% oil in its seeds, mostly ricinoleic acid, an unusual hydroxy fatty acid
Launches seeds from explosive capsules, then ants carry them off by their fatty caruncle
Grows several metres in a single season
edibilityNote: Seeds are deadly if chewed or crushed: ricin causes symptoms after a delay of several hours, including severe vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, dehydration, low blood pressure and failure of the liver, kidneys and spleen; a few well-chewed seeds can kill a child. Swallowed whole seeds may pass through intact. Commercial castor oil is ricin-free. Seeds are used in jewellery and are attractive to children; also highly toxic to dogs.

uses.use: Castor oil as a laxative and in ointments
Castor oil (eranda taila) as a purgative and for joint pain (vata disorders)
Castor oil is an approved stimulant laxative; ricinoleic acid also used in drug formulations

medicinal.cautions: Castor oil can cause cramps and diarrhoea and can trigger uterine contractions; avoid in pregnancy unless medically supervised. Never ingest seeds.

fruit.description: Three-lobed, spiny green-to-red capsules that split explosively.

seed.description: Glossy seeds mottled brown, black and white, with a pale caruncle
seed.germination: Soak overnight and sow in warmth (with gloves); 1–3 weeks

steps: Wear gloves and keep seeds away from children and pets
Soak seed overnight and sow indoors in warmth
Plant out after frost in rich soil
Remove flower spikes before seeds form if children or animals visit

lore: Castor seeds have been found in Egyptian tombs from about 4000 BCE, and Herodotus described Egyptians using 'kiki' oil in lamps. In 1978 Bulgarian dissident Georgi Markov was killed in London by a tiny ricin pellet fired, it is believed, from a modified umbrella.
funFact: 'Ricinus' is Latin for 'tick', because the seeds look like a swollen tick.

summary: The poison that killed Socrates. Poison hemlock looks like a tall, lacy wild carrot or parsley, but every part contains coniine and related alkaloids that paralyse muscles from the legs upward, ending in respiratory failure while the mind stays clear.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa and western Asia; invasive in the Americas, Australia and New Zealand
abilities: Makes piperidine alkaloids (coniine, γ-coniceine) that block nicotinic receptors at the nerve–muscle junction
Grows as a biennial to 2–3 m tall, forming dense stands along ditches
Gives off a musty, mouse-like smell when crushed, from its alkaloids
Coniine was the first alkaloid ever synthesised in a lab (by Albert Ladenburg, 1886)
edibilityNote: All parts are deadly, especially seeds and roots; leaves are most toxic in spring before flowering. Symptoms begin 30 minutes to a few hours after eating: burning mouth, salivation, dilated pupils, tremors, then ascending muscle paralysis, slowing heart and death from respiratory failure. Lookalikes: wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace (hairy stem, no purple blotches, carrot smell), parsley, chervil, fennel, cow parsley and wild parsnip. Key signs of hemlock: smooth hollow stem with purple-red blotches and a mousy smell. Even handling can irritate; wash after contact.

uses.use: Applied externally for tumours and swellings and as a sedative; used in Athens as a method of execution

medicinal.cautions: Deadly; no safe home use.

fruit.description: Small, grey-brown ribbed fruits with wavy ridges, in umbels.

seed.germination: Not for cultivation; controlled as a noxious weed in many places

lore: Plato's Phaedo describes Socrates' death in 399 BCE after drinking hemlock, the numbness creeping upward from his feet. Hemlock was named among the ingredients of the witches' brew in Macbeth: 'Root of hemlock digg'd i' the dark'.
funFact: Migrating quail that eat hemlock seeds have reportedly poisoned people who ate the birds, a syndrome called coturnism.

summary: Often called the most toxic plant in North America. Water hemlock's thick, chambered roots contain cicutoxin, which triggers violent seizures within as little as 15 minutes. A piece of root the size of a walnut can kill a 550 kg cow, and people have died after eating only small amounts.
nativeRange: Most of North America, from Canada to Mexico
abilities: Makes cicutoxin, which blocks GABA-A receptors in the brain and causes uncontrolled seizures
Stores most toxin in thickened, chambered roots that ooze yellowish oily liquid when cut
Grows in wet ground where it can be confused with edible wetland plants
Is toxic enough to kill cattle that eat a few roots exposed by ploughing or flooding
edibilityNote: All parts are deadly, most of all the roots and stem base, especially in spring. Symptoms within 15–60 minutes: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, frothing at the mouth, then violent seizures, irregular heartbeat and death from respiratory failure; survivors may have lasting muscle and memory problems. Lookalikes: water parsnip (Sium suave), wild parsnip, wild carrot, angelica, cow parsnip and edible wetland roots. Key sign: chambered (hollow with cross-walls) root crown and leaf veins ending in the notches between teeth rather than at the tips.

fruit.description: Small round ribbed fruits in loose umbels.

seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: Colonial writers and Indigenous traditions alike recorded water hemlock as a deadly poison, and it was a long-feared killer of cattle on the American frontier, where roots exposed by spring floods or ploughing were eaten by stock.
funFact: Children have been poisoned by using the hollow stems as peashooters or whistles.

otherNames: Fùzǐ 附子 / Wūtóu 乌头 (Chinese, for related species)
summary: A stately garden perennial with hooded blue-violet flowers, and one of the most poisonous plants in Europe. Aconitine can enter through the skin and causes tingling and numbness, vomiting, and deadly heart rhythms. Greek myth said it grew from the saliva of Cerberus.
nativeRange: Mountains of western and central Europe
abilities: Makes aconitine, which locks sodium channels open in nerves and heart muscle
Its hooded flowers can be opened only by long-tongued bumblebees
Stores toxin-rich tuberous roots that replace themselves each year
Alkaloids can be absorbed through broken skin when handled
edibilityNote: All parts are deadly, especially roots and seeds. Within minutes to an hour: tingling and numbness of the mouth and face spreading to limbs, nausea, vomiting, sweating, weakness, then dangerous ventricular arrhythmias and death. Roots have been mistaken for horseradish or other roots, and leaves for wild greens. Wear gloves when handling; gardeners have been poisoned through the skin. No antidote; treatment is supportive.

uses.use: Tincture of aconite as a pain reliever and fever remedy (now abandoned)
Processed roots of Aconitum carmichaelii (fuzi) used for 'cold' conditions; processing reduces toxicity
