medicinal.cautions: Potentially fatal, even in herbal products; poisoning from improperly processed aconite herbs is still reported in Asia.

fruit.description: Clusters of three to five dry pods that split along one side.

seed.germination: Needs cold stratification; slow

grow.timeToHarvest: Ornamental; flowers in 2–3 years from seed
steps: Always wear gloves when planting, dividing or cutting
Plant tubers in moist, rich soil in partial shade
Keep away from vegetable beds and places children or pets play
Label clearly; never plant near horseradish or other edible roots

lore: Ovid's Metamorphoses tells how aconite sprang from the foam of Cerberus when Hercules dragged him from the underworld. The name 'wolfsbane' comes from its use in baits and arrow poisons for wolves.
funFact: The 'monk's hood' is a sepal, not a petal; the true petals are reduced to two hidden, nectar-holding spurs inside it.

otherNames: Manzanilla de la muerte ('little apple of death', Spanish)
summary: Often called the most dangerous tree in the world. Its small green apple-like fruits burn the mouth and throat, its milky sap blisters skin, and sheltering under it during rain can cause burns as sap is washed off the leaves. It still does important work holding Caribbean beaches together.
nativeRange: Southern Florida, the Caribbean, the Bahamas, Central America and northern South America
abilities: Its latex contains phorbol esters that cause severe blistering of skin and eyes
Stabilises sandy beaches and dunes with dense roots and windbreak crowns
Tolerates salt spray, storms and nutrient-poor sand
Fruits float, spreading the tree along coasts by sea
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic. Eating the sweet-smelling fruit causes intense burning, blistering and swelling of the mouth and throat, vomiting and bloody diarrhoea; historical accounts describe deaths, though modern documented fatalities are rare. Sap causes blistering dermatitis and can cause temporary blindness; rain dripping from the leaves and smoke from burning wood are also harmful. Lookalike: crab apples or guava. Trees are often marked with red bands or warning signs.

fruit.description: Small green to yellowish fruits like crab apples, with a pleasant smell.

seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: The Spanish called it 'manzanilla de la muerte', and Caribbean peoples reportedly used its sap on arrows; legend says Juan Ponce de León died in 1521 after being wounded by such an arrow in Florida.
funFact: Some animals are unaffected: the black spiny-tailed iguana (Ctenosaura similis) eats the fruit and even lives among the branches.

summary: A climbing legume whose glossy scarlet seeds with black eyes are strung into rosaries, necklaces and toys, and contain abrin, a toxin even more potent than ricin. The hard coat usually protects a swallowed whole seed, but a single chewed or crushed seed can be fatal.
nativeRange: Tropical Asia and probably tropical Africa and Australia; naturalised widely, invasive in Florida and the Caribbean
abilities: Makes abrin, a protein that disables ribosomes, as ricin does
Its hard, waterproof seed coat lets seeds survive for years
Its leaves contain glycyrrhizin and are sweet, like liquorice
Fixes nitrogen and climbs over other vegetation
edibilityNote: Seeds are deadly if chewed, crushed or broken (drilling seeds for jewellery has poisoned craftspeople). After a delay of hours to days: severe vomiting, bloody diarrhoea, dehydration, seizures and failure of liver, kidneys and other organs. Whole seeds swallowed intact often pass harmlessly. Leaves are chewed as a sweetener in India, but the plant should not be eaten; keep seed jewellery away from children.

uses.use: Seeds used only after 'purification' (shodhana) by boiling in milk, and roots and leaves for coughs and sore throats
Leaf tea for coughs and colds

medicinal.cautions: Seeds can be fatal; traditional detoxification is not reliable for home use.

fruit.description: Short pods that curl open to show red-and-black seeds.

seed.description: Glossy scarlet seed with a black spot at the hilum
seed.dispersal: Birds attracted by the bright seeds (which offer no food reward)
seed.germination: Not recommended: invasive and toxic

lore: In India the seeds served goldsmiths as a unit of weight, the ratti (about 0.12 g), and the Sanskrit name gunja appears in Ayurvedic texts that prescribe elaborate purification before any use.
funFact: In 2012 the Eden Project in Cornwall withdrew bracelets from its shop after it emerged they were strung with rosary pea seeds.

summary: Europe's ancient churchyard tree, some individuals possibly 2,000 years old or more, and one of its most poisonous. Its needles and seeds contain taxine alkaloids that can stop the heart, yet its needles are also the starting material for the cancer drug docetaxel.
nativeRange: Europe, North Africa (Atlas Mountains), western Asia to northern Iran
abilities: Lives for many centuries; the Fortingall Yew in Scotland is estimated at 2,000–3,000 years
Regrows from old wood and can send down internal roots inside its hollow trunk
Tolerates deep shade and heavy pruning, which makes it ideal for hedges and topiary
Its elastic heartwood and springy sapwood made the best longbows
edibilityNote: Everything except the red fleshy aril is deadly; the seed inside the aril is toxic if chewed, so arils should not be eaten. Needles (fresh or dried) contain taxine B, causing dizziness, dry mouth, dilated pupils, vomiting, slow or irregular heartbeat and sudden cardiac arrest, sometimes within hours. Clippings are deadly to horses and cattle. Lookalikes: other dark conifers; children may eat the sweet red berries.

uses.use: 10-deacetylbaccatin III from yew needles is used to semi-synthesise docetaxel and paclitaxel, chemotherapy drugs for breast, lung and prostate cancers
Leaves used for respiratory complaints

medicinal.cautions: Raw plant material is deadly; taxane drugs are given only under specialist care.

fruit.description: Bright red, juicy cups with a single dark seed visible at the opening.

seed.description: Hard, dark seed in a red aril
seed.dispersal: Thrushes and other birds eat the arils and pass the seed
seed.germination: Needs warm then cold stratification; often takes two years

steps: Take semi-ripe cuttings in late summer
Plant in well-drained soil; yew dies in waterlogged ground
Clip annually for hedges or topiary
Never let livestock or horses near clippings

lore: The Clacton spear, about 400,000 years old and among the oldest known wooden artefacts, is made of yew, and Ötzi the Iceman carried a yew longbow. In Britain yews were planted in churchyards, and Shakespeare's Macbeth includes 'slips of yew' in the witches' cauldron.
funFact: Paclitaxel (Taxol) was first found in the bark of the Pacific yew in the 1960s; making it from European yew needles meant trees no longer had to be stripped of bark.

summary: A rank, weedy nightshade with large white trumpet flowers and spiny seed pods, packed with tropane alkaloids that cause terrifying delirium. It takes its English name from Jamestown, where soldiers who ate it in 1676 reportedly behaved like fools for eleven days.
nativeRange: Probably North and Central America; now a cosmopolitan weed
abilities: Makes scopolamine, hyoscyamine and atropine, which block acetylcholine receptors
Opens fragrant flowers at dusk for hawkmoth pollinators
Produces seed that stays alive in soil for decades
Thrives in disturbed, fertile ground and contaminates grain and vegetable crops
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic, especially seeds. The anticholinergic syndrome ('blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, red as a beet, hot as a hare, dry as a bone') includes dilated pupils, blurred vision, flushed hot dry skin, fast heart, urinary retention, hallucinations and delirium, seizures and sometimes death. Poisoning has happened through seeds contaminating buckwheat, soy or millet, leaves mistaken for other greens, and deliberate use as a hallucinogen. Physostigmine is used as an antidote under medical care.

uses.use: Purified dhatura used for asthma, pain and skin disease
Leaves smoked in 'asthma cigarettes' for bronchospasm

medicinal.cautions: Potentially fatal; dose varies hugely between plants. Purified atropine and scopolamine are approved drugs, but the plant itself is not safe to use.

fruit.description: Walnut-sized green capsules covered in spines that split into four to release many seeds.

seed.dispersal: Falls from the capsule; carried in contaminated grain
seed.germination: Not recommended for cultivation

lore: Robert Beverley's History and Present State of Virginia (1705) describes soldiers at Jamestown who ate the plant in salad and spent days in a foolish delirium. In Hindu tradition dhatura flowers and fruits are offered to Shiva.
funFact: Seeds of Datura can lie in the soil for over 30 years, waiting for the ground to be disturbed.

summary: A pretty woodland wildflower that killed thousands of American settlers indirectly. Cattle grazing it pass its toxin, tremetol, into their milk, and people who drank the milk developed 'milk sickness', which killed Abraham Lincoln's mother, Nancy Hanks Lincoln, in 1818.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America
abilities: Makes tremetol (a mixture including tremetone), a toxin that builds up in the milk and meat of grazing animals
Flowers in late summer and autumn, feeding bees, butterflies and moths when few flowers remain
Grows well in shade where most toxic forage plants do not
Spreads by seed and short rhizomes into woodland colonies
edibilityNote: Leaves and stems are toxic to livestock (horses, cattle, sheep, goats), causing 'trembles'. People are poisoned indirectly by drinking milk or eating meat from poisoned animals: weakness, vomiting, tremors, severe constipation, acetone-smelling breath, and in serious cases death. Modern milk pooled from many farms is not a risk. Lookalikes: boneset (Eupatorium perfoliatum) and other white-flowered Eupatorium species.

uses.use: Root tea used for diarrhoea, kidney stones and fevers, and the root as a snakebite poultice (as the name suggests)

medicinal.cautions: Toxic; not for internal use.

fruit.description: Tiny black achenes with white hairs.

seed.description: Small black achene with a white pappus
seed.germination: Cold-stratify; self-sows freely

steps: Sow in autumn or cold-stratify seed
Plant in shade where it can naturalise
Keep out of any pasture used by livestock
Deadhead to limit self-seeding

lore: Milk sickness devastated frontier settlements in Ohio, Indiana and Illinois in the early 1800s; Dr. Anna Pierce Hobbs Bixby of Illinois is credited, in local tradition, with identifying the plant in the 1830s with help from a Shawnee woman. The cause wasn't accepted by science until the 1920s.
funFact: Milk sickness cases have mostly vanished since farms began pooling milk from many herds.

otherNames: Tsuta-urushi ツタウルシ (Japanese, for East Asian forms)
summary: A vine, shrub or ground cover whose oily resin, urushiol, causes an itchy, blistering rash in most people. Urushiol stays active on clothes, tools and pet fur for a long time. To wildlife it is a valuable plant: dozens of bird species eat its pale berries in winter.
nativeRange: Eastern and central North America, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean; related forms in East Asia
abilities: Produces urushiol, which triggers allergic contact dermatitis in most people
Grows as a ground cover, shrub or high-climbing vine with hairy aerial roots
Feeds songbirds, woodpeckers and wild turkeys with fat-rich winter berries
Grows faster and makes more potent urushiol under higher CO₂, experiments show
edibilityNote: All parts contain urushiol: leaves, stems, roots and berries, in all seasons, even dead plants. Touching causes an itchy red rash with blisters 12–72 hours later. Burning it releases urushiol in smoke, which can cause severe lung and eye inflammation. Eating any part is dangerous. Lookalikes: Virginia creeper (five leaflets), boxelder seedlings, fragrant sumac and young raspberry or blackberry; 'leaves of three, let it be' is a good guide. Wash skin with soap and cool water soon after contact.

fruit.description: Clusters of small, waxy, greyish-white berries.

seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: Captain John Smith described it at Jamestown in 1609, comparing it to English ivy and recording that it caused 'redness, itchiness, and lastly blisters'. Urushiol is named after urushi, the lacquer from the related Asian lacquer tree.
funFact: In a Duke University experiment, poison ivy grown at elevated CO₂ grew bigger and made a more allergenic form of urushiol.

summary: A monster of a plant up to about 5 m tall, with umbrella flower heads up to a metre across, introduced to Europe and North America as a Victorian ornamental. Its sap makes skin dangerously sensitive to sunlight, causing burns and blisters that can scar for years.
nativeRange: Western Greater Caucasus; invasive across Europe, Canada and the northern United States
abilities: Its sap contains furanocoumarins that bind DNA when struck by UV light, causing phytophotodermatitis
Grows to about 5 m tall with umbels up to a metre across
Produces thousands of seeds per plant (often around 20,000), which spread along rivers
Lives several years as a leafy rosette, then flowers once and dies
edibilityNote: The sap in all parts, especially stems and leaves, contains furanocoumarins (e.g. bergapten, psoralens). On skin followed by sunlight, it causes burns and blisters within 24–48 hours, leaving dark patches and sensitivity for months or years; sap in eyes can cause temporary or lasting blindness. Do not eat any part. Lookalikes: native cow parsnip (Heracleum maximum or H. sphondylium), angelica, wild parsnip and poison hemlock. If exposed, wash immediately and keep out of sunlight for 48 hours.

fruit.description: Flat, oval, ribbed fruits with brown oil channels.

seed.dispersal: Wind and water, often along rivers
seed.germination: Do not plant: it is a legally controlled invasive species in many countries

lore: Seeds from the Caucasus were listed at Kew Gardens in 1817 and it was planted in Victorian gardens as a spectacle. Genesis recorded 'The Return of the Giant Hogweed' (1971), a mock-epic about the plant taking revenge on Britain.
funFact: It is named after Paolo Mantegazza, a 19th-century Italian physician, physiologist and anthropologist.

summary: Australia's most painful plant, a nettle relative whose heart-shaped leaves are covered in hollow, silica-tipped hairs. A sting can cause excruciating pain that flares for days or weeks, and in some cases months. In 2020 researchers found the cause: tiny peptide toxins they named gympietides.
nativeRange: Rainforests of north-eastern Queensland, Australia; also eastern Indonesia (Moluccas) and Papua New Guinea
abilities: Covers its leaves, stems and fruit with silica-tipped hollow hairs that inject toxin like hypodermic needles
Makes gympietides, peptide toxins that act on pain-sensing sodium channels, similar to spider and cone snail toxins
Is a pioneer that quickly fills rainforest gaps after storms or clearing
Its hairs stay able to sting in dried herbarium specimens for decades
edibilityNote: Every surface of the plant stings. Contact causes intense burning pain, swelling and redness, with flare-ups from touch, cold or water for weeks; severe stings have caused collapse. The pink-purple fruits are eaten by animals but stinging hairs make them dangerous for people. Remove hairs with wax strips or adhesive tape, not by rubbing; seek medical help for large stings.

fruit.description: Mulberry-like clusters of pink to purple fruits, also covered in hairs.

seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: The name gympie-gympie comes from the language of the Gubbi Gubbi (Kabi Kabi) people of south-eastern Queensland, and early settler accounts reportedly tell of horses driven mad by the stinger. Australian ecologist Marina Hurley, who studied the plant, described being stung as like being 'burnt with hot acid and electrocuted at the same time'.
funFact: Despite its stings, Dendrocnide leaves are eaten by red-legged pademelons and certain beetles, which seem unaffected.

summary: A shrub with huge, nodding white trumpets that perfume the night air, popular in gardens worldwide. It is no longer known in the wild: every Brugmansia species is listed as Extinct in the Wild, possibly because the animal that spread its seeds vanished. All parts carry scopolamine and related alkaloids.
nativeRange: Atlantic Forest of south-eastern Brazil (now known only in cultivation and as escapes)
abilities: Produces scopolamine, hyoscyamine and atropine in all tissues
Releases strong evening scent to attract night-flying moths
Grows flowers up to about 30 cm long
Survives today only through human cultivation
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous, especially seeds and leaves. Eating any part, or tea from flowers, causes an anticholinergic delirium: dilated pupils, blurred vision, fast heart, hot dry skin, confusion, terrifying hallucinations, amnesia and sometimes death. Rubbing an eye after handling flowers can cause one dilated pupil for hours to days. Teenagers using it as a 'legal high' are often hospitalised. Similar-looking Datura is equally toxic.

fruit.description: Smooth, spindle-shaped green fruits, rarely produced in cultivation.

seed.dispersal: Unknown in the wild; possibly extinct animal dispersers
seed.germination: Usually grown from cuttings

grow.timeToHarvest: Flowers in the first or second year
steps: Wear gloves and wash hands after handling
Root cuttings in water or moist mix in warmth
Feed and water heavily while growing
Keep away from children and pets; bring indoors before frost

lore: Brugmansia species have long been used by Andean and Amazonian shamans as powerful and dangerous visionary plants. Long classified in Datura, angel's trumpets were split out by Christiaan Persoon in 1805 as Brugmansia, named after Dutch naturalist Sebald Justinus Brugmans.
funFact: Brugmansia flowers hang down, whereas Datura flowers point up; this is the easiest way to tell them apart.

summary: A tree whose disc-shaped seeds contain strychnine, one of the most notorious poisons in history. Strychnine blocks inhibitory glycine receptors in the spinal cord, so muscles convulse uncontrollably while the victim stays fully conscious.
nativeRange: India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
abilities: Makes strychnine and brucine, mostly in its seeds (about 1–1.5% strychnine)
Produces orange, apple-sized fruits whose pulp birds such as hornbills eat while discarding the seeds
Its alkaloids are so bitter that strychnine can be tasted at extremely low dilutions
Grows in dry and moist forests across the Indian subcontinent
edibilityNote: Seeds are deadly; bark, leaves and root also contain strychnine and brucine. Within 15–60 minutes: anxiety, muscle twitching, then violent convulsions triggered by any noise or touch, arching of the back (opisthotonus), a fixed grin (risus sardonicus) and death from respiratory failure or exhaustion, while the person stays conscious. The fruit pulp is sometimes described as edible but is risky and not recommended.

uses.use: Seeds (kupilu) used only after purification in cow's urine, milk or ghee, in tiny doses for nerve and digestive disorders
Processed seeds (ma qian zi) for pain and paralysis
Strychnine used as a 'tonic' and stimulant

medicinal.cautions: Deadly; poisonings from traditional preparations are still reported. No safe home use.

fruit.description: Smooth, hard-shelled orange fruit with white jelly-like pulp and several seeds.

seed.dispersal: Birds and monkeys eating the pulp
seed.germination: Not for cultivation

lore: Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou isolated strychnine in 1818. At the 1904 St Louis Olympics, marathon winner Thomas Hicks was given strychnine and brandy by his trainers during the race and nearly collapsed.
funFact: Strychnine's complex structure took until 1946 to work out (Robert Robinson), and R. B. Woodward first synthesised it in 1954.

summary: The source of about 90% of the world's cotton. Each fibre is a single seed-coat cell that can grow to about 3 cm long. Domesticated in Mesoamerica thousands of years ago, it became the crop at the centre of the Industrial Revolution and the transatlantic slave economy.
nativeRange: Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean (wild forms on coasts); cultivated worldwide
abilities: Grows single-celled seed hairs up to about 3 cm long, the cotton fibre
Is an allotetraploid that combines two ancient genomes, one from Africa/Asia and one from the Americas, which merged 1–2 million years ago
Defends itself with gossypol-filled glands visible as black dots on leaves and seeds
Feeds ants and other insects with extrafloral nectaries on leaves and bracts
edibilityNote: Refined cottonseed oil is widely eaten. Raw seeds contain gossypol, which is toxic, can damage the liver and reduce fertility, and is especially harmful to pigs, poultry and young animals. A low-gossypol cotton variety (TAM 66274) was cleared by US regulators in 2018–2019 for food use.

uses.tradition: Traditional medicine in the American South
uses.use: Root bark used to bring on menstruation or abortion, including by enslaved women
Gossypol tested in thousands of men as a male contraceptive; abandoned due to permanent infertility and low potassium

medicinal.cautions: Gossypol is toxic; root bark preparations may cause miscarriage.

fruit.description: Green bolls that split into three to five sections to release fluffy white lint around seeds.

seed.description: Dark seeds covered in long lint and short fuzz
seed.dispersal: Wind and water for wild forms; humans for crops
seed.germination: Sow 2–3 cm deep in soil above 18 °C; 1–2 weeks

grow.zones: Annual in USDA 7–11; perennial in frost-free areas
steps: Sow after soil warms in late spring
Thin to 15–30 cm apart in full sun
Water through flowering and boll set
Pick lint from open bolls in dry weather

lore: Cotton textiles in Mexico's Tehuacán Valley date back thousands of years, and the Aztecs collected cotton cloth as tribute. Eli Whitney's 1793 cotton gin made upland cotton hugely profitable, fuelling the expansion of slavery in the American South.
funFact: A cotton seed sprouted on the far side of the Moon aboard China's Chang'e 4 lander in 2019, the first plant to grow there, though it died soon after.

summary: The source of indigo, the dye of blue jeans and once one of the world's most valuable trade goods. The leaves are green; the blue appears only when they are fermented in water and the liquid is beaten with air, turning the colourless indican into insoluble blue indigotin.
nativeRange: Uncertain due to ancient cultivation; probably tropical Asia or Africa; grown across the tropics
abilities: Stores indican, a colourless glycoside, which turns into blue indigo when fermented and exposed to air
Fixes nitrogen in root nodules, so it was used as a soil-improving crop
Regrows after cutting, allowing several leaf harvests a year
edibilityNote: Not eaten. Some Indigofera species (e.g. Indigofera spicata) are poisonous to livestock; I. tinctoria should not be eaten.

uses.use: Leaves (nili) in hair oils for hair growth and greying, and for liver and skin complaints
Indigo pigment (qing dai, mostly from other plants) for skin and inflammatory conditions

medicinal.cautions: Internal use is not well studied; avoid in pregnancy.

fruit.description: Thin, straight brown pods with small seeds.

seed.germination: Soak or scratch seed; sow in warmth, 1–2 weeks

steps: Scarify and soak seed, then sow in warm soil
Grow in full sun with moderate water
Cut leafy stems just before flowering
Steep leaves in water for 12–24 hours, add lime, then beat in air until it turns blue

lore: The Greeks called the dye 'indikon', 'from India'. The Bengal Indigo Revolt of 1859 and the play Nil Darpan (1860) protested forced indigo growing, and Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, at Champaran in 1917, defended indigo farmers.
funFact: Adolf von Baeyer worked out indigo's structure and synthesis by 1883, and BASF's synthetic indigo from 1897 destroyed the plant indigo trade within a few decades.

summary: One of humanity's first crops, giving both linen and linseed oil. Its bast fibres are among the strongest plant fibres, and dyed wild flax fibres from a cave in Georgia are about 30,000 years old. The seeds are rich in omega-3 fatty acids and fibre.
nativeRange: Domesticated in the Fertile Crescent from wild Linum bienne; cultivated worldwide
abilities: Produces long, strong bast fibres used for linen, rope and fine paper
Its seeds are rich in α-linolenic acid (an omega-3) and lignans
Its oil dries to a tough film, the basis of oil paints, putty and linoleum
Its seed coat makes mucilage when wet, which swells to many times its volume
edibilityNote: Seeds are widely eaten. They contain cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin); normal amounts are safe, but very large quantities of raw or unripe seed should be avoided. Drink plenty of water with ground seed, since it swells. Linseed oil sold for wood finishing is not food-grade.

uses.use: Whole or cracked seed as a bulk laxative; poultices for skin inflammation
Seeds (atasi) for cough, constipation and skin conditions
Ground flaxseed studied for lowering blood pressure and cholesterol

medicinal.cautions: Can block the gut if taken without enough water; may slow absorption of other medicines; caution with bowel obstruction.

fruit.description: Round capsules with ten shiny seeds.

seed.description: Flat, glossy brown or golden seeds
seed.dispersal: Capsules mostly stay closed on modern cultivars; harvested by people
seed.germination: Sow 1–2 cm deep in cool spring soil; 5–10 days

grow.timeToHarvest: Fibre at ~90 days; seed at ~100–120 days
steps: Broadcast seed thickly in early spring
Keep weeded in the first weeks
For fibre, pull whole plants when lower stems yellow, and rett them in dew or water
For seed, harvest when capsules are brown and rattle

lore: Ancient Egyptians wrapped mummies in linen and called it 'woven moonlight'. Dzudzuana Cave in Georgia yielded dyed wild flax fibres around 30,000 years old, among the oldest known fibres used by people.
funFact: The species name usitatissimum means 'most useful' in Latin.
